items.explanation: Bradford governed Plymouth for decades and was no dissenter. Williams was banished and founded Rhode Island, Hutchinson was tried and exiled, and Hooker led followers to Connecticut — all broke with Massachusetts Bay orthodoxy.
items.stem: Who among the following was NOT a religious dissenter from Massachusetts Bay?

option_explanations.A: Correct — Bradford is the exception. He was the longtime governor of Plymouth Colony, a separate colony from Massachusetts Bay, and was never a dissenter from it.
option_explanations.B: Williams was a genuine Massachusetts Bay dissenter: the General Court banished him in 1635 for challenging its authority, and he founded Rhode Island as a haven for religious dissent.
option_explanations.C: Hutchinson was a genuine dissenter: Massachusetts Bay tried her in 1637 for her religious teachings and banished her.
option_explanations.D: Hooker was a dissenter in practice: he led his congregation out of Massachusetts Bay in 1636 to found Hartford and Connecticut, rejecting the Bay Colony's government.

items.explanation: Cecilius Calvert, the second Lord Baltimore, received the Maryland charter in 1632 and founded the colony as a haven for persecuted English Catholics.
items.stem: The colony founded as a refuge for English Catholics was

option_explanations.A: Pennsylvania was founded as a refuge for Quakers, not Catholics — William Penn, a Quaker, received its charter in 1681.
option_explanations.B: South Carolina was founded by English planters from Barbados as a plantation colony; it had no Catholic-refuge purpose.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Cecilius Calvert — the second Lord Baltimore — received the Maryland charter in 1632 and founded the colony as a haven for English Catholics, who faced persecution at home.
option_explanations.D: Virginia was founded as a commercial venture to profit the Virginia Company, and its established church was Anglican — not a Catholic refuge.

items.explanation: English migrants were pushed by crowded cities and religious conflict and pulled by the chance to prosper — through land, tobacco, fish, furs, and timber — in the New World.
options: A. Dislike of the Church of England
items.stem: English men and women crossed the Atlantic in the 1600s because of

option_explanations.A: This was a real motive: Puritans, Separatists, and Catholics all crossed the Atlantic to escape religious conflict and the established Church of England — but it was only one of several causes.
option_explanations.B: This was a real motive: enclosure and economic dislocation pushed poor and landless English out of crowded cities and villages — but it was only one of several causes.
option_explanations.C: This was a real motive: land, tobacco, fishing, furs, and timber pulled migrants seeking to better their fortunes — but it was only one of several causes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. English migration had both push factors (crowded cities, religious conflict) and pull factors (economic opportunity), so 'all of the above' captures the full picture.

items.explanation: English colonies were typically chartered to companies or proprietors and quickly developed elected assemblies, unlike the tightly crown-controlled Spanish and French empires.
options: A. They were not ruled directly by the crown
B. They granted rights to Native peoples
D. They were more thinly populated
items.stem: Early English colonies differed most sharply from Spanish and French colonies in that they

option_explanations.A: Correct. English colonies were typically chartered to companies or proprietors and quickly developed elected assemblies, whereas the Spanish and French empires were administered directly by crown-appointed officials.
option_explanations.B: The English did not grant rights to Native peoples. English settlement steadily displaced Native peoples from their land — the opposite of extending them rights.
option_explanations.C: English colonies were not economic failures: tobacco made Virginia and Maryland profitable, and New England thrived on fishing, timber, and trade.
option_explanations.D: English colonies were more densely populated than the French and Spanish ones, with tens of thousands of settler families — the reverse of 'thinly populated.'

items.explanation: Like the Compact, the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) was a written agreement by which settlers constituted a government and defined its powers -- colonial America's first experiments in creating government by written consent. The Bill of Rights limited an existing monarchy, the Proclamation restricted settlement, and the Olive Branch Petition sought reconciliation; none founded a government the way the Compact and the Orders did.
options: A. The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639)
B. The English Bill of Rights (1689)
items.stem: Which of the following most closely resembled the Mayflower Compact as an act of creating government by written agreement?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James... Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation..."
—Mayflower Compact, 1620 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like the Compact, the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) was a written agreement by which settlers constituted a government and defined its powers — America's first written constitution and the closest match to a people creating government by written agreement.
option_explanations.B: The English Bill of Rights (1689) limited an existing monarchy and protected Parliament's rights; it did not found a government by agreement the way the Compact did.
option_explanations.C: The Proclamation of 1763 forbade settlement west of the Appalachians to avoid conflict with Native peoples; it restricted colonists rather than creating a government.
option_explanations.D: The Olive Branch Petition (1775) asked George III for reconciliation with the colonies; it was an appeal to authority, not an act of creating government.
